what it does

the brain is about 86 billion neurons joined by something like 100 trillion connections, and it is the system most ideas in machine learning were first borrowed from.

the machine echo

pick a region to see which part of modern ai resembles it, and where the resemblance stops.

( 01 · two kinds of neuron )

01 / 04

a real neuron spikes. an artificial one returns a number. turn up the input and they start to agree.

membrane voltage · leaky integrate-and-firefiring 0 hz

current flows in and charges the cell like a leaky bucket. when the voltage reaches −55 mv the neuron fires a spike, resets, and starts filling again. stronger input means faster spikes.

output vs inputinput 2.20 na
biological firing rateartificial neuron (relu)
2.20 na

below about 1.5 na nothing happens: the leak drains charge as fast as it arrives. above that threshold, the firing rate climbs with the input. the relu function used in most modern networks, zero below a threshold and a straight line above it, is a deliberately crude copy of that curve.

the copy throws away almost everything: spike timing, the shape of each cell, chemistry, and the fact that one real neuron can receive ten thousand inputs on branches that compute things of their own. it keeps the one idea that turned out to matter most for learning: a unit that stays quiet until its input is strong enough, then responds in proportion.

( 03 · fire together, wire together )

03 / 04

draw a path through the network, again and again. it will start to remember it.

move across the network. each neuron you touch fires and sends a pulse to its neighbours. when one neuron fires just before another, the connection between them gets stronger. that is hebb's rule, proposed in 1949 and still the oldest idea about how learning happens in the brain.

trace the same route a few times. once a connection is strong enough, touching the first neuron sets off the rest of the chain by itself: a memory. unused connections slowly fade back.

strong synapses0

( 04 · where the analogy breaks )

04 / 04
i.

spikes, not numbers

neurons talk in timed pulses, and the timing itself carries information. most artificial networks pass smooth numbers forward one layer at a time and ignore time completely.

ii.

no obvious backprop

training a network sends an exact error signal backwards through every layer. nobody has found that mechanism in the brain. local learning rules, feedback connections and dopamine-like teaching signals are the leading candidates, and it is still an open question.

iii.

learning never stops

you learn all day without erasing yesterday. a network trained on something new tends to overwrite what it knew before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. the hippocampus and sleep seem to be part of how brains avoid it.

iv.

a body, on 20 watts

a brain learns while living in a body that moves, eats and is rewarded or hurt by the world, and it does so on roughly the power of a dim light bulb. models learn from fixed datasets on hardware that draws far more.
